newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - LTV sees more acquisitions.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - LTV sees more acquisitions.

text.p: LTV Corp will likely continue its recent pattern of acquiring or taking partial ownership interests in steel-related businesses to deliver more consistent earnings and profitable growth, David Hoag, LTV chairman, said Thursday.

"What we're up to here is trying to get more consistent earnings and trying to get a higher return on our capital, which you know is a struggle, always, in the steel business," Hoag told Reuters in an interview at the American Iron and Steel Institute's annual meeting.

LTV, the third largest U.S. integrated steelmaker, in recent months has acquired steel-related businesses that focus on processing and downstream operations. LTV also has taken partial ownership in such businesses, including a 25 percent stake in a steel slitting and blanking operation in Mexico.

Major U.S. steelmakers within the past year have been purposefully shifting their product mix toward selling more processed and finished steel products, which are more profitable than commodity products such as hot-rolled sheet.
Hoag said LTV is continuing to seek acquisition opportunities.

"We're not doing this helter skelter. There are specific strategic purposes for each of these acquisitions," Hoag said. "We're not going to do anything dumb...we look at hundreds of opportunities all the time. It's an ongoing process and we'll just keep looking."

Separately, Hoag said consolidation within the U.S. steel industry is probably necessary to help steelmakers raise prices with their major customers. But he added that any type of large merger in the industry is not likely to happen anytime soon.
"I think we're in the very beginning stages of starting to evaluate what might make sense for these various companies," he said.

The U.S. steel industry has been void of merger activity for at least a decade, but in recent months the industry's top executives -- including USX Corp's U.S. Steel Group President Paul Wilhelm and Inland Steel Industries Inc Chairman Robert Darnall -- have said consolidation could give steelmakers more pricing leverage with their biggest customers, including the three major U.S. automakers.
There are at least half a dozen steelmakers supplying automakers. That has given automakers the ability to keep a lid on the prices they pay for steel.

"I think now is the time to begin looking at (consolidation,") Hoag said. "I would suspect that over the next couple of years there will be much more talk about this than there has been. I think there are probably too many of us," he said. "I think (consolidation) would make sense, but only if there are (operational) synergies. If there can be major cost savings, then it ought to happen. If there can't be major cost savings, then it shouldn't happen."
Commenting on current domestic market conditions, Hoag characterized the market as strong but said it has weakened slightly in recent months, partially due to lower car sales.
"It's not as strong as it was six or nine months ago," he said. "We have customers shutting down for a week, either because their inventories are too high or they don't have the orders.
"Volume is good and will continue to be good, but not as strong as it was over the last couple of years."
LTV and its competitors have raised steel prices twice so far this year, once in January and again in May.
Hoag said those increases have held only partially in the market. "It's an ongoing struggle," he said.
Hoag declined to comment on earnings projections. Wall Street's consensus estimate for 1997 is $1.03 per share, versus $1.01 last year.

He said '97 is shaping up to be a profitable year. "But it is a struggle to make the cost to capital, which is what we are desperately trying to do," he said. "Most of the industry did not make it last year...we have a ways to go before we are satisfied."
